source: Ellamil, Dobson, Beeman, Christoff (2012) Evaluative and generative modes of thought during the creative process
finding: Founding human fMRI study (abstract only read via Europe PMC). Participants designed book covers, alternating generation and evaluation. Generation recruited medial temporal lobe. Evaluation recruited executive and default regions plus rostrolateral PFC, insula, temporopolar cortex. Executive and default regions stayed positively coupled throughout.
numbers: Abstract gives no N or effect sizes; Europe PMC lists 291 citations.
quote: creative evaluation may extend beyond deliberate analytical processes
limits: Abstract only. Drawing task, designers, small fMRI sample. Phases were self-paced and alternated, so they are not fully pure.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that judging an idea is a different mode from producing it, and is partly affective, not only analytic. This is the source analogy for separate generate and judge calls (G5, G8). It does not show an LLM judge has the affective part.

source: Beaty et al. (2015) Default and executive network coupling supports creative idea production
finding: Abstract read via Europe PMC. Divergent thinking recruited default and executive hubs. Default-salience coupling came early in the task, default-executive coupling later. Network efficiency rose with divergent-thinking ability.
numbers: No numbers in abstract. 349 citations per Europe PMC.
limits: Abstract only. Divergent thinking task, not generate/evaluate alternation. Shows coupling, not strict separation.
agent_relevance: Suggests production and control cooperate over time, so a clean split is a simplification. The scaffold split is a design choice, not a brain fact.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review of human ideas versus LLM ideas made with a generate-many then rank pipeline. LLM ideas were judged more novel, slightly weaker on feasibility. A human re-rank of the LLM ideas scored higher still.
numbers: 79 reviewers, 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84, AI 5.64, AI + human rerank 5.81 (p<0.05). Overall score per review: human 4.68, AI 4.85, AI + rerank 5.34 (p=0.04 for rerank vs human).
limits: Ideas only, not executed. Style was normalised by an LLM. 7 NLP topics. Reviewer agreement is low (c04).
agent_relevance: Large generation pool plus a separate selection step can reach expert-judged novelty. But the human rerank beat the model rerank, so the selector is the weak part.

source: Si et al. (2024) section 7.2: LLMs cannot evaluate ideas reliably
finding: LLM judges were tested on ranking the top and bottom 25 percent of ideas by expert score. All were at or near chance, and below the agreement between human reviewers.
numbers: Balanced accuracy: human split-half 56.1%, NeurIPS-21 66.0%, ICLR-24 71.9%. GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3% (best), AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Small balanced set of 98 ideas. Human labels are themselves noisy. Pairwise ranking on ICLR papers gave 71.4% for Claude-3.5, so judgement is easier on papers than on raw ideas.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G8: a model opinion on novelty is near chance. The agent must not let an LLM be the final selector of ideas.

source: Si et al. (2024) sections 3.2, 3.3, 7.1: overgeneration and ranking pipeline
finding: The agent generated 4000 seed ideas per topic, deduplicated by embedding similarity, then ranked. Duplication, not quality, caps the benefit of generating more.
numbers: Dedup at cosine 0.8 left about 5% unique (200 of 4000). Pairwise ranker trained as a proxy on 1200 ICLR 2024 submissions: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%. Top-10 vs bottom-10 gap in ranker score rose with rounds (0.56 at N=1 to 0.97 at N=3).
limits: Ranker proxy is accepted-vs-rejected papers, not novelty of ideas.
agent_relevance: Generate wide, dedupe in code, rank in pairs. Pairwise comparison worked better than direct scores. Matches the code-selects guardrail.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Expert Ideas
finding: 43 experts each spent over 100 hours executing a randomly assigned idea. After execution, the LLM ideas lost much more score than human ideas, and in several metrics the ranking flipped. Pre-execution scores did not predict post-execution scores well.
numbers: N=43 executors. Drop larger for AI ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall (p<0.05). Ideation-to-execution Spearman correlations weak, e.g. 0.077 for one cell and -0.148 for another; AI ideas show a moderately negative correlation on excitement.
limits: Same 7 NLP topics, one generator (Claude-3.5-Sonnet pipeline). Execution scores come from another reviewer set.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence for G8: judging an idea by reading it does not predict how it does when run. Novelty should be tested by execution or a code check.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts, appendix B.2 generation versus evaluation split
finding: On Game of 24 the generator and the evaluator were swapped between GPT-4 and GPT-3.5. A strong generator with a weak evaluator kept most of the gain. The reverse did not.
numbers: GPT-4 ToT 74%; GPT-3.5 ToT 19%; GPT-4 generation + GPT-3.5 evaluation 64%; GPT-3.5 generation + GPT-4 evaluation 31%. Plain CoT scored 4% in the headline comparison with GPT-4.
limits: One puzzle with a checkable answer. Evaluator here is a value prompt (sure/maybe/impossible), not an open idea judge.
agent_relevance: Gives a measured split: generation quality was the bottleneck, and a cheaper judge can be used. Supports separate calls with different models for propose and judge.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without oracle labels, asking a model to review and fix its own answer does not help and often hurts. Reported gains in earlier papers came from using the true label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 then 74.7 over rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 then 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5 vs 95.5 standard. GSM8K: 74.7% of the time GPT-3.5 kept its answer; it changed correct to incorrect more often than the reverse.
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only; external feedback and tools are not covered. Models from 2023.
agent_relevance: A model judging its own output is not a reliable evaluator. A separate judge with no access to the earlier answer, or an external check, is needed (G5, G10).

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 critiquing itself collapsed performance in Game of 24, graph colouring and planning. A sound external verifier gave large gains, and re-prompting with just the verifier's yes/no kept most of the gain.
numbers: Game of 24: standard prompting 5%, LLM+LLM critique 3%, LLM + sound verifier 36-38%. Verifier alone via pure rejection with k=25 reached 42%. When the LLM verifies equations that equal 24 it labels 79.1% correct; it also labels 81.6% as evaluating to 24.
limits: GPT-4 era models; three planning-style domains with exact checkers.
agent_relevance: Verification is not easier than generation for the model itself. Use code verifiers for any claim that can be checked; the critique text adds little.

source: Song et al. (2025) Mind the Gap: Examining the Self-Improvement Capabilities of LLMs
finding: Defines a generation-verification gap (how much a model's own verifier improves its own generations). The relative gap rises with pre-training compute for good verification methods (chain-of-thought score) but not for others. It saturates to zero in a few rounds of iteration, and effective diversity falls.
numbers: Gap scales monotonically with pre-training FLOPs for CoT-Score and tournament verification, roughly linear in log FLOPs (conjectured). Cross-verification: gap grows with verifier strength, shrinks with generator strength. Many models show no self-improvement on tasks beyond their ability.
limits: Verification of answers with checkable labels (maths, QA), not creative ideas.
agent_relevance: A stronger or different model as judge helps more than self-judging. Iterating generate-then-judge loops runs out after a few rounds.

source: Li et al. (2023) Benchmarking and Improving Generator-Validator Consistency of LMs
finding: Models answer a question correctly but then reject their own answer when asked to validate it. Fine-tuning on consistent pairs raised consistency and also improved generation and validation.
numbers: GPT-4 consistent 76% of the time; text-davinci-003 and GPT-4 about 75.8-79.1% per task; Alpaca-30B 60% to 93-94% after consistency fine-tuning. Across 6 tasks generator quality +16%, validator accuracy +6.3%. Novel tasks (plan arithmetic, prompt prioritization) only about 60%, near the 50% chance level.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, so not a prompt-only fix. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: The same model's generating and judging roles disagree a lot, which is a reason to keep them as separate calls and not trust one to ratify the other.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) Self-[In]Correct: LLMs Struggle with Discriminating Self-Generated Responses
finding: Tested the premise that discriminating among earlier outputs is easier than generating. Across several open and industrial models and tasks, discrimination was not reliably better than generation, and often worse.
numbers: No single headline figure; reported as a metric comparing discrimination accuracy with generation accuracy across models and tasks (Table 6 and conclusion).
limits: Models of 2024; formats of answer choice. Exact per-model figures were not extracted in this session.
agent_relevance: The human intuition that judging is easier than producing does not transfer to LLMs. Do not count on a judge pass to repair weak generation.

source: West et al. (2023) The Generative AI Paradox: What It Can Create, It May Not Understand
finding: Models match or beat humans at generating, but fall short at discriminating or answering questions about the same content. Human understanding tracks generation more tightly than the model's does.
numbers: GPT-4 picks the correct answer 100% of the time against easy negatives but drops with hard negatives; humans stay near 85-100% on hard cases. Gap widens with task difficulty (XSUM, Dialog tasks). Image side: humans 92.9-100%, CLIP models 50-76% on hard discriminative cases.
limits: 2023 models; selective and interrogative tasks on language and images.
agent_relevance: In models, generation and judgement are partly independent skills. This is the opposite of the human pattern and is a reason to measure the judge separately.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Models can tell their own text from others at above chance, and the stronger this self-recognition, the more they prefer their own text as judges. Fine-tuning to recognise self raised the bias in a linear way.
numbers: GPT-4 and Llama 2 over 50% self-recognition out of the box; GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 over 90% after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Summarisation tasks (XSUM, CNN/DM).
limits: Summarisation; correlation shown, with fine-tuning controls for causation.
agent_relevance: A judge must not see authorship. Same-model generate and judge will favour its own ideas. Hide the source and use a different model or code (G5).

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: Strong LLM judges agree with human preferences at the level of human-human agreement, but show position bias, verbosity bias and some self-enhancement.
numbers: Over 80% agreement with humans. GPT-4 favours itself with a 10% higher win rate and Claude-v1 with a 25% higher win rate than human judges give; GPT-3.5 shows no self-favouring. On the repetitive-list attack, GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 prefer the longer repeated answer; GPT-4 resists.
limits: Authors state the data could not settle self-enhancement. General chat tasks, not novelty.
agent_relevance: Judges work for chat quality but carry known biases. Control position, length and authorship in any judge call.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
finding: Swapping the order of two responses reverses LLM-judge verdicts. A calibration framework reduced it.
numbers: With ChatGPT as judge, Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries (82.5%) in the favourable order. Vicuna-13B vs ChatGPT win rate swung from 51.3% to 23.8% when the order flipped. Proposed remedies: multiple evidence calibration, balanced position calibration, human in the loop.
limits: Vicuna benchmark, 80 queries; 2023 judges.
agent_relevance: Always run both orders and combine in code. This is cheap and matches G5.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) keeps growing with the number of samples. Where a verifier exists, this turns into accuracy. Where it does not, majority vote and reward models plateau near 100 to several hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, above the 43% single-sample best. A math task rises to 98.44% coverage with 10,000 samples while vote and reward-model selection plateau at about 100 samples.
limits: Domains with automatic verification show the gain. Reward model used was ArmoRM-Llama3-8B.
agent_relevance: Generating widely is cheap. The bottleneck is the selector. For open ideas without a verifier, selection is where the loss happens.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: A trained process reward model (step-level judge) picked better solutions than an outcome reward model or majority vote.
numbers: MATH subset, best-of-1860: process-supervised PRM 78.2%, outcome-supervised ORM 72.4%, majority voting 69.6%. PRM800K step labels released.
limits: Trained verifier on human step labels; maths only.
agent_relevance: A dedicated judge trained or prompted on steps beats a vote. Needs labelled data or a checker, so it is not available for open creative tasks.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Human-like Diversity
finding: 20 leading models give much less distinct output than humans. Larger models in a family often produce less diversity. Asking for creativity barely helps; showing the model its earlier answers and asking for a different one nearly matches humans.
numbers: Most models produce fewer than 3 distinct responses in 10 queries; Gemma 2-2B and Llama 3.2-1B were most diverse. Human baseline: 8 authors per prompt on 100 curated prompts. In-context regeneration with Claude-3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro roughly matched human diversity; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro beat human cumulative utility. Equivalence classifier 79% accurate versus human labels.
limits: Human baseline is 8 paper authors, a homogeneous group; they note this lower-bounds human diversity.
agent_relevance: Generation step: have the model see its prior ideas and be told to diverge, in one context. Selection of a distinct set is then a judging problem in code or by a separate call.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Different models give strikingly similar open-ended answers. Reward models and LLM judges are worse calibrated to humans on pairs of similar quality or where annotators disagree.
numbers: 26K queries; 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item. Average pairwise embedding similarity within one prompt typically above 0.8 at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0. Cross-model similarity 71% to 82%. Spearman correlation of judges with human average drops on similar-quality and high-disagreement subsets.
limits: Embedding similarity measures surface and semantic overlap, not value. Judge calibration shown on rating tasks.
agent_relevance: Using a different model as judge does not give an independent view, as models share biases. Judges are weakest exactly where choosing among near-equal ideas matters.

source: McAleese et al. (2024) LLM Critics Help Catch LLM Bugs
finding: A critic model trained with RLHF to write feedback on code caught more bugs than paid human reviewers. Model critiques were preferred over human critiques. Critics also hallucinated bugs. Human plus critic teams hallucinated less.
numbers: Model critiques preferred over human critiques in 63% of cases on code with naturally occurring LLM errors. Critic found hundreds of errors in ChatGPT training data rated flawless.
limits: Trained critic, code tasks.
agent_relevance: A judge that is trained or set up for the judging role, not the generator, adds value. Pair critique with a second check to cut invented problems.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompting or supervised fine-tuning on correction traces rarely teaches self-correction. Multi-turn RL on the model's own data did.
numbers: Self-correction gain of 15.6% on MATH (Gemini 1.0 Pro) and 9.1% on HumanEval (Gemini 1.5 Flash).
limits: Needs training, not a scaffold.
agent_relevance: Confirms that a prompt scaffold alone is not enough for self-judging. Our no-training agent should lean on external checks.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Self-repair gains were modest and varied once the cost of repair is counted, and the bottleneck is the model's feedback on its own code. A stronger feedback model gave much larger gains.
numbers: Code Llama, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS; gains sometimes absent. GPT-4 given human feedback did much better than GPT-4 self-feedback (exact figures not extracted).
limits: Code tasks with test feedback.
agent_relevance: The weakest step in generate-then-fix is the judge's feedback. Put the strongest model or a real test in the judge slot.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: Automated LLM reviewer was reported as near human on predicting paper decisions. Later work (c04) found the same style of reviewer near chance on raw ideas.
numbers: Human NeurIPS balanced accuracy 0.66, F1 0.49, AUC 0.65. Sonnet 3.5 0.52, GPT-4o-mini 0.53, GPT-4o 0-shot 0.61, GPT-4o 1-shot 0.60 (uncalibrated rows); with reflection and ensembling the best reviewer is said to reach F1 0.57 and AUC 0.65.
limits: Tested on past ICLR papers, which may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Reviewer-agent success on papers does not carry to judging unproven ideas. Treat reported judge accuracy with care.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Ideas: Revolutionizing Research via Novel Idea Development with LLM Agents
finding: An agent that builds a literature chain before generating ideas. It is judged in a pairwise round-robin 'Idea Arena' where an LLM judge was compared with human researchers.
numbers: Reported 56 Elo points over the second-best method in human evaluation; human evaluation used 10 researchers pairwise.
limits: Judge-based arena; novelty by LLM and human opinion, no execution.
agent_relevance: Example of an agent loop that splits retrieval, generation and arena-style judging. Its judge scores carry the weaknesses in c04 and c06.

source: Weng et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
finding: Only the abstract opening was read. Proposes backward verification where the model checks its answer by masking a condition and reconstructing it. Claimed gains in arithmetic and commonsense.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Reported gains conflict with later no-oracle self-correction results (c08, c09). Not checked here.
agent_relevance: A narrow, structured check (backward reconstruction) may work where free-form self-critique does not. Needs checking before use.

source: Meta-analysis of fMRI studies of two creativity subsets in divergent thinking (2022), Europe PMC record 35906880
finding: Located only by title: a meta-analysis of fMRI studies on two creativity subsets in divergent thinking. Not read.
numbers: 16 citations per Europe PMC.
limits: Title only; authorship and results not verified.
agent_relevance: Lead for the human-side group to pull; not used for design.
